article.title: Why Your Inner Thighs Are Super Important!
article.sourceNote: Source: Teacher-provided classroom source image. Citation/source label reproduced as supplied.
paragraphs: Did you know that your inner thighs do a lot more than just help you kick a soccer ball?
They’re called adductors, and they help keep your body stable when you walk, run, or jump! These muscles help pull your legs together and are important for keeping your balance.
If they’re weak, you could end up with aches and pains, especially in your lower back or knees. This can happen to anyone, from athletes to kids who sit too long at school!

To strengthen your adductors, try some fun exercises like the bridge with squeeze, where you lie on your back with a pillow between your knees and lift your hips, or the side-lying leg lift, where you carefully lift your lower leg while lying on your side. Strengthening your inner thighs can help you move better and feel great, so give it a try!

mainIdeaQuestion.title: Main Idea Question
mainIdeaQuestion.question: Which statement best summarizes the main idea of Source WP?
options: The inner thigh muscles, called adductors, support stability and balance, and strengthening them with simple exercises can help prevent weakness-related discomfort and improve movement.
Soccer players are the only people who need strong inner thighs because kicking a ball is the main function of the adductors.
Kids who sit at school should avoid walking, running, and jumping until a doctor treats their knees and lower back.
The bridge with squeeze is much harder than the side-lying leg lift and requires special gym equipment.

feedback.correct: Correct! Source WP explains what adductors do for stability and balance, what could happen if they are weak, and how two simple exercises can strengthen them.
feedback.incorrect: Check all four paragraphs: Source WP defines adductors, explains their role in movement and balance, notes possible aches from weakness, and introduces two simple exercises.

mainIdeaQuestion.explanation:
Option A is correct (O): Source WP introduces the inner thighs as adductors (P1–P2), explains that they keep the body stable, pull the legs together, and support balance (P2), warns that weak adductors could lead to aches and pains in the lower back or knees for athletes or students who sit too long (P3), and suggests two exercises to strengthen them so you can move better and feel great (P4).
Option B is incorrect (X): Paragraph 1 specifically says inner thighs "do a lot more than just help you kick a soccer ball," and Paragraph 3 says weakness can happen to anyone, including kids at school.
Option C is incorrect (X): Source WP never advises avoiding walking, running, or jumping, nor does it mention doctors or medical treatment.
Option D is incorrect (X): Source WP calls both "fun exercises" and uses a simple pillow rather than gym equipment, without comparing their difficulty.

readingComprehension.title: Reading Comprehension
readingComprehension.instructions: Answer all 6 questions using only the information stated in Source WP.

questions.question: According to Paragraphs 1 and 2, what are your inner thigh muscles called, and what does the article say about kicking a soccer ball?
options: They are called lower legs, and kicking a soccer ball is the only thing they do.
They are called adductors, and they do much more than just help you kick a soccer ball.
They are called lower backs, and they only work when you sit at school.
They are called bridges, and they are used only by professional soccer athletes.
questions.explanation:
Option B is correct (O): Paragraph 1 asks whether inner thighs "do a lot more than just help you kick a soccer ball?" and Paragraph 2 identifies them: "They’re called adductors."
Option A is incorrect (X): "Lower leg" refers to the leg lifted in the side-lying leg lift (P4), not the name of the inner thigh muscles, and P1 states they do "a lot more."
Option C is incorrect (X): "Lower back" is a body area where aches and pains could happen (P3), not the muscle name.
Option D is incorrect (X): "Bridge with squeeze" is an exercise name (P4), not the muscle name.

questions.question: According to Paragraph 2, when do the adductors help keep your body stable?
options: Only when you lie on your back with a pillow
Only when you sit at a desk for a long time
When you walk, run, or jump
Only when you kick a soccer ball
questions.explanation:
Option C is correct (O): Paragraph 2 states directly: "they help keep your body stable when you walk, run, or jump!"
Option A is incorrect (X): Lying on your back with a pillow describes the bridge with squeeze exercise in Paragraph 4.
Option B is incorrect (X): Sitting too long at school is mentioned in Paragraph 3 as a situation linked to weakness, not stability.
Option D is incorrect (X): Paragraph 1 says they do "a lot more than just help you kick a soccer ball."

questions.question: Besides keeping your body stable, what other two things does Paragraph 2 say these muscles help do?
options: Lift your hips and bend your lower back
Pull your legs together and keep your balance
Stretch your arms and strengthen your neck
Protect your pillow and speed up your sitting

Option A is incorrect (X): Lifting your hips is an action in the bridge with squeeze (P4), and bending the lower back is not mentioned.
Option C is incorrect (X): Arms and neck are not mentioned anywhere in Source WP.
Option D is incorrect (X): This mixes unrelated words from Paragraphs 3 and 4.

questions.question: According to Paragraph 3, what could happen if your adductors are weak, and who can this happen to?
options: You could get aches and pains in your lower back or knees, and it can happen to anyone from athletes to kids who sit too long at school.
You will permanently lose your ability to walk, and it only happens to older adults.
You will feel pain only in your shoulders, and it only affects professional runners.
You will immediately break a knee bone, and it only happens when playing soccer.
questions.explanation:
Option A is correct (O): Paragraph 3 states: "If they’re weak, you could end up with aches and pains, especially in your lower back or knees. This can happen to anyone, from athletes to kids who sit too long at school!"
Option B is incorrect (X): Source WP says you "could end up with aches and pains," never claiming permanent loss of walking or limiting it to older adults.
Option C is incorrect (X): Shoulders are never mentioned, and Paragraph 3 explicitly says "anyone," including kids at school.
Option D is incorrect (X): Broken bones are never mentioned in Source WP.

questions.question: How do you perform the bridge with squeeze according to Paragraph 4?

You sit in a chair at school and press your knees against a desk.

Option B is incorrect (X): Lying on your side is part of the side-lying leg lift, and even there you lift your lower leg, not your top leg.
Option C is incorrect (X): Sitting at school is mentioned in Paragraph 3, not as an exercise in Paragraph 4.

questions.question: According to Paragraph 4, how do you do the side-lying leg lift, and what is the article’s final message?
options: You lie on your back and lift both legs quickly; doing this cures all knee injuries forever.
You carefully lift your lower leg while lying on your side; strengthening your inner thighs can help you move better and feel great.
You jump as high as possible; athletes must do this exercise every hour at school.
You squeeze a pillow while walking; inner thighs only matter during soccer games.

Option A is incorrect (X): You lie on your side (not your back) and lift carefully (not quickly), and Source WP never promises a cure for all injuries.

languageFocus.title: Language Focus: Definitions, Conditionals, Purpose & Exercise Descriptions
languageFocus.topic: Explaining Body Functions, Cause/Effect, and Exercise Steps from Source WP
languageFocus.explanation: Source WP uses clear, accessible informational grammar to define a body part, show what happens under certain conditions, explain purpose, and describe exercise steps accurately.

patterns.name: 1. Definition / Naming Structure ("They’re called...")
patterns.explanation: Introduces a specific term for something already familiar to the reader.
patterns.example: The muscles on the inside of the legs are called adductors.
patterns.sourceExample: They’re called adductors, and they help keep your body stable when you walk, run, or jump!

patterns.name: 2. Cause and Effect ("could end up with...", "can help you...")
patterns.explanation: Shows possible results cautiously using modals like "could" and "can" instead of guaranteed medical promises.
patterns.example: Without regular movement, students could end up with discomfort, whereas simple exercises can help them move comfortably.
patterns.sourceExample: If they’re weak, you could end up with aches and pains, especially in your lower back or knees. / Strengthening your inner thighs can help you move better and feel great, so give it a try!

patterns.name: 3. Time Clauses with "when" and "while"
patterns.explanation: Connects muscle function or exercise action to the exact moment an activity happens.
patterns.example: Your leg muscles work together when you jump and while you hold an exercise pose.
patterns.sourceExample: ...they help keep your body stable when you walk, run, or jump! / ...where you carefully lift your lower leg while lying on your side.

patterns.name: 4. Conditional Clause with "if"
patterns.explanation: States a condition (weak adductors) and its possible consequence (aches and pains).
patterns.example: If your inner thighs are weak, your knees or lower back could feel sore.
patterns.sourceExample: If they’re weak, you could end up with aches and pains, especially in your lower back or knees.

patterns.name: 5. Purpose Infinitive ("To strengthen...")
patterns.explanation: Begins a sentence with "To + base verb" to explain why someone performs the exercises.
patterns.example: To strengthen your inner thighs, you can practice slow, controlled floor exercises.
patterns.sourceExample: To strengthen your adductors, try some fun exercises like the bridge with squeeze...

patterns.name: 6. Relative Clauses with "where..."
patterns.explanation: Adds a clear step-by-step description directly after the name of an exercise.
patterns.example: One simple exercise is the bridge with squeeze, where you place a pillow between your knees.
patterns.sourceExample: ...the bridge with squeeze, where you lie on your back with a pillow between your knees and lift your hips, or the side-lying leg lift, where you carefully lift your lower leg while lying on your side.

patterns.name: 7. Action Verbs for Movement and Exercises
patterns.explanation: Uses clear, concrete verbs to show everyday movement and exact exercise instructions.
patterns.example: People kick, walk, run, and jump every day, and during exercises they lie down and lift carefully.
patterns.sourceExample: ...kick a soccer ball... / ...walk, run, or jump! / ...pull your legs together... / ...lie on your back... and lift your hips... / ...carefully lift your lower leg while lying on your side.

writingTask.modelAnswer: According to Source WP, the inner thigh muscles are called adductors and are essential for daily movement. To strengthen the adductors, Source WP suggests two exercises: the bridge with squeeze, where you lie on your back with a pillow between your knees and lift your hips, and the side-lying leg lift, where you carefully lift your lower leg while lying on your side. Overall, strengthening your inner thighs can help you move better and feel great.

teacherNotes.topic: Core Source Terms Coverage (10 Target Items)
teacherNotes.note: Ensure students distinguish all 10 terms in context: inner thighs (inside upper legs), adductors (inner thigh muscles), stable (steady during movement), balance (staying upright), aches and pains (general soreness/discomfort), lower back (bottom of back), strengthen (make stronger), bridge with squeeze (back-lying, pillow between knees, lift hips), side-lying leg lift (side-lying, lift lower leg), and lower leg (the leg closer to the floor when lying on your side).

teacherNotes.topic: Separating Source Claims from Teacher Explanation
teacherNotes.note: Explicitly model the boundary between what Source WP states (functions, possible aches and pains in lower back or knees, two exercises) and teacher-provided grammar/ESL scaffolding (how "if", "when", "to strengthen", and "where" clauses work). Students must attribute claims to Source WP rather than stating them as personal medical expertise.

teacherNotes.topic: Non-Medical Caution: No Diagnosis or Treatment Guarantees
teacherNotes.note: Source WP is a general informational fitness reading, NOT medical advice. Highlight the author’s cautious modals: "could end up with aches and pains" and "can help you move better and feel great." Explicitly forbid students from writing medical diagnoses, clinical claims, or cure guarantees (e.g., do NOT write "this cures knee injury" or "sitting causes permanent damage").

For G1 students, provide sentence frames ("According to Source WP, adductors are...", "If they are weak, ...", "To strengthen them, ...") and highlight the two "where..." exercise descriptions visually. For G2 students, challenge them to combine the two exercises with "whereas" or "while" and maintain consistent cautious attribution throughout a 115–130 word paragraph.

teachingScript.objective: Activate everyday awareness of leg movement, balance, and sitting fatigue without requiring prior anatomy knowledge.
actions: Display the Lesson Header title ("Why Your Inner Thighs Are Super Important!") and source note.
Preview the 3 Warm-up questions on leg movement, balance, and weak muscles from sitting.
teachingScript.scriptEn: Good morning, class. / Today we are reading Source WP: / "Why Your Inner Thighs Are Super Important!" / Before we read, look at the three Warm-up questions. / You do not need any medical or anatomy terms yet. / Just think about kicking a ball, / keeping your balance, / and how your body feels after sitting at school.
teachingScript.scriptKo: 안녕하세요, 여러분. / 오늘 우리는 Source WP인 / "Why Your Inner Thighs Are Super Important!"를 읽을 것입니다. / 읽기 전에 세 가지 워밍업 질문을 보세요. / 아직 의학 용어나 해부학 지식이 전혀 필요하지 않습니다. / 공을 차는 것, / 균형을 잡는 것, / 그리고 학교에 오래 앉아 있을 때 몸이 어떤지 일상 경험으로 생각해 보세요.
teachingScript.studentActions: Students read the 3 Warm-up prompts, discuss briefly with a partner, or jot short answers using the sentence starters.
teachingScript.misconception: Students may worry that they do not know medical muscle names before reading.
teachingScript.correctiveFeedback: Reassure students that Warm-up focuses only on everyday movement, balance, and comfort; the text itself will introduce the muscle name.
teachingScript.transition: Now let us preview the 10 key vocabulary terms from Source WP so every phrase in the reading feels clear.

teachingScript.objective: Build student familiarity with all 10 required vocabulary terms, especially exercise phrases and movement nouns.
actions: Model pronunciation for "adductors", "stable", "aches and pains", "strengthen", and "side-lying leg lift".
Check comprehension of "lower back" vs. "lower leg" and confirm "side-lying leg lift" keeps its hyphen.
teachingScript.scriptEn: Let us look at the ten vocabulary items in context. / First, notice the muscle name: "adductors." / Say it with me: ad-DUC-tors. / Next, look closely at two phrases that both contain the word "lower": / "lower back" means the bottom part of your back, / while "lower leg" in the side-lying leg lift / means the leg underneath, closer to the floor. / Also notice that "side-lying leg lift" stays hyphenated.
teachingScript.scriptKo: 이제 문맥 속 어휘 10개를 살펴봅시다. / 먼저 근육 이름인 "adductors(내전근)"를 보세요. / 함께 따라 읽어 봅시다: ad-DUC-tors. / 다음으로, 둘 다 "lower"가 들어가는 두 표현을 구별해 봅시다: / "lower back"은 허리 아래쪽을 뜻하고, / side-lying leg lift에서의 "lower leg"는 / 옆으로 누웠을 때 바닥에 가까운 아래쪽 다리를 뜻합니다. / 또한 "side-lying leg lift"에는 하이픈(-)이 유지된다는 점도 확인하세요.
teachingScript.studentActions: Students repeat key words aloud, check Korean meanings, and underline "lower back" vs. "lower leg" in their notes.
teachingScript.misconception: Students often confuse "lower leg" (below the knee vs. bottom leg when lying on one’s side) or omit the hyphen in "side-lying".
teachingScript.correctiveFeedback: Clarify that in Source WP’s side-lying leg lift, "lower leg" means the bottom leg resting on the floor while lying on your side.
teachingScript.transition: With these 10 terms clear, let us read the exact Source WP passage for the gist.

teachingScript.phaseName: Gist Reading (Exact Source WP & Main Idea)
teachingScript.objective: Read the exact 4-paragraph Source WP passage aloud and verify understanding of the Main Idea.
actions: Read all 4 paragraphs and "Source: WP" aloud in exact canonical form without paraphrasing.
Guide students to select and justify the single best Main Idea option.
teachingScript.scriptEn: Let us read Source WP together / from the title down to "Source: WP." / Follow each paragraph carefully: / Paragraph 1 opens with a question about kicking a soccer ball. / Paragraph 2 names the adductors and explains stability and balance. / Paragraph 3 explains what could happen if they are weak. / Paragraph 4 introduces two exercises to strengthen them. / After reading, answer the Main Idea question.
teachingScript.scriptKo: 제목부터 "Source: WP"까지 / Source WP 본문을 함께 읽어 봅시다. / 각 문단을 주의 깊게 따라오세요: / 1문단은 축구공을 차는 것에 대한 질문으로 시작합니다. / 2문단은 내전근의 이름을 밝히고 안정성과 균형을 설명합니다. / 3문단은 이 근육들이 약할 때 생길 수 있는 일을 설명합니다. / 4문단은 이를 강화하는 두 가지 운동을 소개합니다. / 읽은 뒤 중심 생각(Main Idea) 문제를 풀어 보세요.
teachingScript.studentActions: Students track the 4 paragraphs silently while listening, then select their answer for the Main Idea MCQ.
teachingScript.misconception: Students might pick an option that exaggerates soccer or invents medical advice.
teachingScript.correctiveFeedback: Point back to P1 ("a lot more than just help you kick a soccer ball") and confirm Option A covers all 4 paragraphs.
teachingScript.transition: Now let us examine each sentence in detail and practice finding exact text evidence.

teachingScript.objective: Complete the 6 Reading Comprehension MCQs and 3 Evidence from the Text responses using only Source WP.
actions: Walk through the 6 Comprehension questions and paragraph references.
Have students draft the 3 Evidence responses (function, two problems/groups, compare exercises) and run Check & Compare.
teachingScript.scriptEn: Now move to Reading Comprehension / and Evidence from the Text. / For every answer, stay strictly inside Source WP. / In Evidence 1, find three functions in Paragraph 2. / In Evidence 2, identify the two body areas / and the two groups of people in Paragraph 3. / Notice the word "could": / Source WP does not diagnose or promise a cure. / In Evidence 3, compare the two exercises in Paragraph 4.
teachingScript.scriptKo: 이제 세부 독해(Reading Comprehension)와 / 본문 근거 찾기(Evidence from the Text)로 넘어갑시다. / 모든 답은 반드시 Source WP 본문 안에서만 찾아야 합니다. / 근거 1번에서는 2문단의 세 가지 기능을 찾으세요. / 근거 2번에서는 3문단의 두 신체 부위와 / 두 집단의 사람들을 파악하세요. / "could"라는 단어에 주목하세요: / Source WP는 의학적 진단이나 완치를 보장하지 않습니다. / 근거 3번에서는 4문단의 두 운동을 비교해 보세요.
teachingScript.studentActions: Students answer RC1–RC6, write Evidence 1–3 in the textareas, and click Check & Compare.
teachingScript.misconception: Students frequently state medical absolutes ("weak adductors always cause back injury") instead of matching "could end up with aches and pains".
teachingScript.correctiveFeedback: Remind students to use cautious source phrasing ("could end up with", "can help") and verify 3-word overlap in Check & Compare.
teachingScript.transition: Let us now examine the grammar patterns Source WP uses to explain functions, conditions, and exercise steps.

teachingScript.objective: Teach the 7 Language Focus structures and walk through all 7 sentences of Source WP using chunking and Feynman explanations.
actions: Highlight definition ("called adductors"), cause/effect, "when", "if", purpose ("to strengthen"), "where..." relative clauses, and action verbs.
Guide students through Sentences 1–7 (P1=1, P2=2, P3=2, P4=2) with chunk reading and Korean translation.
teachingScript.scriptEn: Look closely at our Language Focus patterns / using exact sentences from Source WP. / First, "They’re called adductors" gives a clear name. / Second, "when you walk, run, or jump" / tells us the time of movement. / Third, "If they’re weak, you could end up with..." / shows a conditional cause and effect. / Fourth, "To strengthen your adductors" expresses purpose, / and "where you lie on your back..." / uses a "where" clause to explain each exercise step.
teachingScript.scriptKo: Source WP의 실제 문장을 활용한 / Language Focus 문법 패턴을 자세히 봅시다. / 첫째, "They’re called adductors"는 명확한 이름을 제시합니다. / 둘째, "when you walk, run, or jump"는 / 움직임의 시점을 알려줍니다. / 셋째, "If they’re weak, you could end up with..."는 / 조건과 그 가능한 결과를 보여줍니다. / 넷째, "To strengthen your adductors"는 목적을 나타내고, / "where you lie on your back..."는 / "where" 관계절로 각 운동의 동작을 설명합니다.
teachingScript.studentActions: Students read the 7 sentences in slash chunks, underline grammar markers (when, if, to strengthen, where), and review examples.
teachingScript.misconception: Students often misuse "where" as a question word instead of a relative adverb explaining an exercise ("an exercise where you lie...").
teachingScript.correctiveFeedback: Show how "where" connects the exercise name ("bridge with squeeze") directly to the position and action performed during it.
teachingScript.transition: Now let us practice building these exact sentence patterns in Writing Practice.

teachingScript.objective: Have students write 4 focused sentences covering definition, "if" cause/effect, exercise sequence, and exercise comparison.
actions: Guide students through Writing Practice prompts 1–4 (define, "if" cause/effect, sequence, compare).
Have students click Check & Compare to verify word counts, connectors, and model answers.
teachingScript.scriptEn: Now complete the four Writing Practice items. / Item 1 asks you to define adductors / using "called adductors" and "when." / Item 2 asks for an "If..." cause-and-effect sentence / with cautious wording like "could." / Item 3 asks you to sequence one exercise / using "To strengthen" and "where." / Item 4 asks you to compare both exercises / using "while" or "whereas." / Click Check & Compare after each one.
teachingScript.scriptKo: 이제 네 개의 Writing Practice 문항을 작성해 봅시다. / 1번은 "called adductors"와 "when"을 사용해 내전근을 정의하는 문항입니다. / 2번은 "could" 같은 신중한 표현과 함께 / "If..." 원인-결과 문장을 쓰는 것입니다. / 3번은 "To strengthen"과 "where"를 사용해 / 한 가지 운동의 순서를 설명하는 것입니다. / 4번은 "while"이나 "whereas"로 두 운동을 비교합니다. / 각 문항마다 Check & Compare를 눌러 점검하세요.
teachingScript.studentActions: Students draft all 4 practice items, inspect live word counts, and run rule-based Writing Check.
teachingScript.misconception: Students may omit the subject or verb after "whereas/while" or forget to include both exercises in Item 4.
teachingScript.correctiveFeedback: Check that both clauses around "while" or "whereas" have complete subjects and verbs ("you lie on your back... whereas you lie on your side...").
teachingScript.transition: You now have all the building blocks for the 100–140 word Writing Task.

teachingScript.objective: Write a 100–140 word evidence-based paragraph answering the exact Source WP prompt without medical claims.
actions: Display the Writing Task prompt, checklist, and paragraph outline.
Monitor live word counts, connector usage, and non-medical wording as students draft and revise.
teachingScript.scriptEn: You have 18 minutes for the Writing Task. / Answer this exact question: / "Why are the adductors important, / and how can a person strengthen them according to Source WP?" / Check every requirement on your list: / definition and pulling legs together, / stability and balance, / one weakness consequence, / both exercises described accurately, / and a concluding sentence. / Aim for 100 to 140 words, / and stay strictly inside Source WP without medical promises.
teachingScript.scriptKo: 이제 Writing Task를 작성할 18분이 주어집니다. / 다음 정확한 질문에 답하세요: / "Source WP에 따르면 내전근이 왜 중요하며, 어떻게 강화할 수 있는가?" / 체크리스트의 모든 요소를 확인하세요: / 정의와 다리를 모으는 기능, / 안정성과 균형, / 약할 때 생길 수 있는 결과 한 가지 이상, / 두 가지 운동에 대한 정확한 설명, / 그리고 결론 문장입니다. / 100~140단어를 목표로 작성하고, / 의학적 약속 없이 철저히 Source WP 내용만 사용하세요.
teachingScript.studentActions: Students write their 100–140 word paragraph, click Check & Compare, and revise using the feedback and checklist.
teachingScript.misconception: Students may write under 100 words, forget the concluding transition ("Overall,"), or claim exercises "cure" injuries.
teachingScript.correctiveFeedback: Prompt students to check the live word count, verify "side-lying leg lift" spelling, and ensure a clear concluding sentence.
teachingScript.transition: Finish your final edits and move to the Self-Check and Submission bar.

teachingScript.objective: Complete the 6-item Self-Check, verify student name and code, and submit work.
actions: Walk through all 6 Self-Check criteria (understanding, vocabulary, function, evidence, exercise description, word count).
Confirm every student enters their Name and Student Code and submits cleanly.
teachingScript.scriptEn: Before clicking Submit, / review all six Self-Check boxes: / Did you show clear understanding of Source WP? / Did you use lesson vocabulary? / Did you explain adductor function and stability? / Did you include evidence without medical claims? / Did you describe both exercises accurately? / And is your paragraph 100 to 140 words? / Enter your Student Name and Student Code, / then click Submit.
teachingScript.scriptKo: 제출(Submit)을 누르기 전에 / 여섯 가지 자가 점검(Self-Check) 항목을 모두 확인하세요: / Source WP를 정확히 이해했나요? / 핵심 어휘를 사용했나요? / 내전근의 기능과 안정성을 설명했나요? / 의학적 과장 없이 본문 근거를 포함했나요? / 두 운동을 정확히 묘사했나요? / 그리고 단어 수가 100~140단어 사이인가요? / 학생 이름과 학생 코드를 입력한 뒤 / 제출 버튼을 누르세요.
teachingScript.studentActions: Students tick all 6 Self-Check items, enter their name and student code, and click Submit.
teachingScript.misconception: Students sometimes click Submit before entering their Student Code or checking their final word count.
teachingScript.correctiveFeedback: Verify Name and Student Code are filled in and confirm whether the submission banner reports cloud or local save.
teachingScript.transition: Great work today explaining movement evidence clearly and responsibly from Source WP.

teachersOpeningScript.label: Opening 1 — Introducing Source WP
teachersOpeningScript.english: Welcome, Grade 9. / Today we are reading Source WP, / titled "Why Your Inner Thighs Are Super Important!" / We will discover what these muscles do / when you walk, run, jump, or keep your balance.
teachersOpeningScript.korean: 9학년 여러분 환영합니다. / 오늘 우리는 "Why Your Inner Thighs Are Super Important!"라는 제목의 / Source WP를 읽습니다. / 걷고, 달리고, 점프하거나 균형을 잡을 때 / 이 근육들이 어떤 역할을 하는지 알아볼 것입니다.
teachersOpeningScript.teachingPurpose: Orient students to the exact title and practical movement focus of Source WP without requiring prior anatomy.

teachersOpeningScript.label: Opening 2 — Source Boundaries & Non-Medical Framing
teachersOpeningScript.english: Remember our reading rule: / we explain only what Source WP says. / Notice the author uses cautious words / like "could end up with" and "can help," / so we do not add outside medical diagnoses or promises.
teachersOpeningScript.korean: 우리의 읽기 규칙을 기억하세요: / 오직 Source WP에 나온 내용만 설명합니다. / 저자가 "could end up with(~할 수도 있다)"와 "can help(도움이 될 수 있다)"처럼 / 신중한 표현을 쓴다는 점에 주목하며, / 외부의 의학적 진단이나 완치 약속은 덧붙이지 않습니다.
teachersOpeningScript.teachingPurpose: Establish strict source fidelity and guard against medical overclaims from the very start.

teachersOpeningScript.label: Opening 3 — Reading-to-Writing Bridge
teachersOpeningScript.english: By mastering key movement terms / and grammar tools like "when," "if," "to strengthen," and "where," / you will write a clear 100–140 word explanation / answering why adductors matter and how to strengthen them.
teachersOpeningScript.korean: 핵심 움직임 어휘와 / "when", "if", "to strengthen", "where" 같은 문법 도구를 익혀, / 내전근이 왜 중요하며 어떻게 강화할 수 있는지 설명하는 / 명확한 100~140단어 글을 쓰게 될 것입니다.
teachersOpeningScript.teachingPurpose: Connect vocabulary and grammar scaffolding directly to the Writing Task prompt.

q1.question: When you kick a ball, run, or jump, which parts of your legs do you notice working the most, and how do your legs stay under control?
q1.focus: Everyday Leg Movement (No Prior Anatomy Required)
q1.teacherTalk: Read aloud in chunks: / "When you kick a ball, / run, or jump, / which parts of your legs / do you notice working the most?" / Invite everyday words like "front of legs," "knees," or "inside of legs."
q1.sampleStudentAnswer: When I kick a soccer ball or run quickly, I feel the front and inside of my legs working to keep my legs steady and pointed in the right direction.
q1.followUpQuestion: What happens if your legs swing out too wide when you run or land from a jump?
q1.korean: 공을 차거나 달리거나 점프할 때 다리의 어느 부분이 가장 많이 일한다고 느끼며, 다리가 어떻게 안정적으로 통제되나요?
likelyResponses: I feel my thighs and knees working when I run or kick.
My legs stay straight so I do not slip or fall.
q1.caution: Do not expect or require technical anatomy terms during Warm-up; the text introduces "adductors" in Paragraph 2.
q1.purpose: Bridge to Paragraph 1 and Paragraph 2: kicking a soccer ball vs. keeping your body stable when walking, running, or jumping.

q2.question: In what daily situations or sports is keeping your balance especially important, and what happens when your body loses stability?
q2.focus: Stability and Balance in Everyday Life
q2.teacherTalk: Read in chunks: / "In what daily situations or sports / is keeping your balance / especially important?" / Ask students to think about stairs, sports turns, or standing on one leg.
q2.sampleStudentAnswer: Keeping balance is especially important when I turn quickly in sports or walk up stairs, because losing stability can make me wobble or stumble.
q2.followUpQuestion: How do your left and right legs work together to keep you balanced?
q2.korean: 일상이나 스포츠에서 균형을 잡는 것이 특히 중요한 상황은 언제이며, 몸이 안정성을 잃으면 어떻게 되나요?
likelyResponses: Balance is important in soccer, basketball, or riding a bus.
If I lose stability, my body wobbles.
q2.caution: Keep examples grounded in everyday balance rather than clinical balance disorders.
q2.purpose: Bridge to Paragraph 2: adductors keeping the body stable and pulling the legs together for balance.

q3.question: How might weak muscles or sitting for long hours at school affect how your body feels when you stand up and move?
q3.focus: Muscle Weakness and Sitting Too Long
q3.teacherTalk: Read in chunks: / "How might weak muscles / or sitting for long hours at school / affect how your body feels?" / Connect directly to students’ own school-day experience.
q3.sampleStudentAnswer: If muscles feel weak after sitting at a desk all day, my back or legs can feel stiff or sore when I finally stand up and walk around.
q3.followUpQuestion: Why might both active athletes and students who sit at school need to care for the same muscles?
q3.korean: 근육이 약하거나 학교에서 오래 앉아 있으면, 일어서서 움직일 때 몸의 느낌에 어떤 영향을 줄 수 있을까요?
likelyResponses: My back or knees feel stiff after sitting through classes.
Weak muscles make moving feel uncomfortable.
q3.caution: Remind students to use cautious words ("might", "could") and avoid diagnosing medical problems.
q3.purpose: Bridge to Paragraph 3 and Paragraph 4: weakness causing possible aches and pains in anyone (athletes to students), and simple exercises to strengthen them.

sourceReadingGuide.title: Source WP Reading & Layout Guide
sourceReadingGuide.description: Use Source WP verbatim as supplied. Do not paraphrase, translate inside the reading block, or add outside anatomy/medical facts.
sourceReadingGuide.sourceLayout: Title ("Why Your Inner Thighs Are Super Important!"), followed by 4 prose paragraphs (7 sentences total), and the exact footer label "Source: WP". Outside the reading block, display "Source: Teacher-provided classroom source image. Citation/source label reproduced as supplied."
sourceReadingGuide.paragraphBoundaries: Paragraph 1 has 1 sentence (hook question). Paragraph 2 has 2 sentences (naming adductors and listing functions). Paragraph 3 has 2 sentences (weakness consequences and who is affected). Paragraph 4 has 2 sentences (two exercises and closing encouragement). No divider markers exist.
sourceReadingGuide.hyphenAndApostropheCheck: Preserve curly apostrophes in "They’re" (P2) and "they’re" (P3), and preserve the hyphen in "side-lying leg lift" (P4).
sourceReadingGuide.nonMedicalBoundary: Point out cautious modals ("could end up with", "can help") so students write evidence-based explanations without medical diagnosis or cure promises.

detailedReadingGuide.sourceLayoutNote: Source WP has 1 title, 4 paragraphs, 7 sentences (P1=1, P2=2, P3=2, P4=2), and "Source: WP". No divider marker.

sentenceAnalysis.original: Did you know that your inner thighs do a lot more than just help you kick a soccer ball?
sentenceAnalysis.chunkReading: Did you know / that your inner thighs / do a lot more than / just help you kick a soccer ball?
sentenceAnalysis.directKorean: 여러분은 알고 있었나요 / 여러분의 허벅지 안쪽이 / 훨씬 더 많은 일을 한다는 것을 / 단지 여러분이 축구공을 차도록 돕는 것보다?
sentenceAnalysis.naturalKorean: 여러분의 허벅지 안쪽 근육이 단순히 축구공을 차는 것을 돕는 일보다 훨씬 더 많은 역할을 한다는 사실을 알고 계셨나요?

mustKnowChunks.use: engaging informational opening question to spark curiosity
mustKnowChunks.example: Did you know that simple floor exercises can help your legs stay steady?

mustKnowChunks.chunk: do a lot more than just...
mustKnowChunks.meaning: 단지 ~하는 것보다 훨씬 더 많은 일을 하다
mustKnowChunks.use: comparative phrase showing an underestimated role
mustKnowChunks.example: Your leg muscles do a lot more than just help you stand up.

paragraphOutline: 1. Topic & Definition: Attribute to Source WP, define inner thigh muscles as adductors, and state their importance for daily movement.
2. Functions: Explain that adductors keep the body stable when you walk, run, or jump, pull your legs together, and maintain balance.
3. Weakness Consequence (Cautious): Use "If" and "could" to state that weak adductors could lead to aches and pains in the lower back or knees for athletes or kids sitting too long at school.
4. Both Exercises: Use "To strengthen" and "where" to describe both the bridge with squeeze (back, pillow between knees, lift hips) and the side-lying leg lift (side, carefully lift lower leg).
5. Conclusion: End with "Overall," or "In conclusion," summarizing that strengthening inner thighs can help you move better and feel great (no medical promises).

teacherCorrectionFocus: Verify accurate Source WP attribution ("According to Source WP...") and zero outside anatomy or medical claims.
Check that students include stability/balance, pulling legs together, one weakness consequence, and both exercises.
Correct passive/be-verb omissions ("are called", "are weak") and preposition + gerund errors ("important for keeping").
Confirm exact spelling of "side-lying leg lift", cautious modals ("could", "can"), concluding transition ("Overall,"), and 100–140 word count.
finalWritingSupport.safeWordingGuidance: Keep every student claim grounded strictly in Source WP. Replace medical promises ("cures injury", "prevents disease", "guarantees recovery") with cautious source phrases ("could end up with aches and pains", "can help you move better and feel great").
finalWritingSupport.g1Scaffold: For G1 ESL students: Provide the 5-sentence paragraph frame with target connectors ("According to Source WP,", "when", "If", "To strengthen", "Overall,") and check off the two "where..." clauses as they copy key phrases accurately.
finalWritingSupport.g2Extension: For G2 ESL students: Challenge students to synthesize both exercises in one balanced complex sentence using "whereas" and both "where..." relative clauses while keeping their paragraph concise between 115 and 130 words.
